items.stem: ‘Mussolini came to power mainly because of the weakness of the Liberal state.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: Governments were short-lived coalitions. Liberals failed to deal with post-war economic problems and unrest. Liberal leaders tried to absorb Fascism, as in the 1921 National Bloc. Against: Fear of socialism drove elites to support Fascism. Fascist violence and organisation. Mussolini's political skill and the king's decision in October 1922. Judgement: the weakness of the Liberal state created the opportunity, but Mussolini came to power because elites afraid of socialism turned to him.

items.stem: The socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti was murdered by Fascists in June 1924. ‘The Matteotti crisis was the turning point in the creation of the Fascist dictatorship.’ How far do you agree?
items.answer: For: It led to the speech of January 1925 and the move to open dictatorship. The opposition's failure removed the last parliamentary challenge. It was followed by the leggi fascistissime. Against: The Acerbo Law and the 1924 election had already given Fascists control of parliament. The dictatorship was built gradually through 1926-28. The support of the king and elites was the decisive factor throughout. Judgement: the Matteotti crisis was the turning point because Mussolini's survival showed that no one would stop him, but it accelerated a process already under way.

items.stem: To what extent was Fascist Italy a totalitarian state by 1929?
items.answer: For: Opposition parties and free trade unions were banned. The press was controlled and OVRA watched dissent. Parliament became a rubber stamp. Against: The king, the Church and the army kept independent power. Mussolini relied on deals with elites. Repression was milder than in Nazi Germany or the USSR. Judgement: Italy was a personal dictatorship by 1929 but not fully totalitarian, because traditional institutions retained power.

items.stem: ‘Fascist economic policies were a failure.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: Quota 90 harmed exports and caused deflation. The Battle for Grain distorted agriculture. Living standards and real wages fell for many workers. Autarky failed to prepare Italy for war. Against: Public works, such as draining the Pontine Marshes, were completed. The IRI saved banks and industries in the Depression. Wheat output and some heavy industry grew. Judgement: Fascist economic policy achieved some propaganda successes and rescued industry in the Depression, but it failed to modernise the economy or prepare Italy for war.

items.stem: Explain one reason why Mussolini survived the Matteotti crisis of 1924.
items.answer: The king refused to dismiss him.

The opposition withdrew from parliament rather than acting. Elites still saw him as a barrier to socialism. items.stem: Lina is planning an answer to the question: “‘The Matteotti crisis was the turning point in the creation of the Fascist dictatorship.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Lina could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the Matteotti crisis was the turning point because Mussolini's survival showed that no one would stop him, but it accelerated a process already under way. Support: It led to the speech of January 1925 and the move to open dictatorship. The opposition's failure removed the last parliamentary challenge. Challenge: The Acerbo Law and the 1924 election had already given Fascists control of parliament. The dictatorship was built gradually through 1926-28.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: A revision guide lists these reasons why the Lateran Agreements were important to Mussolini. A: They increased his international prestige. items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: They increased his international prestige. B: They ended the conflict between the Church and the Italian state since 1870. C: They removed a possible centre of opposition. Possible judgement: they gave the regime a legitimacy that no other policy achieved.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: Study Sources A and B. Source A: Mussolini, speech to the Chamber of Deputies, 3 January 1925 (translated, abridged). “I declare that I, and I alone, assume the political, moral and historical responsibility for all that has happened.” Source B: a letter from a Liberal politician, 1924 (illustrative). “We have left the chamber in protest, but the king will not act and the industrialists still prefer Mussolini to disorder. We have made ourselves powerless.” How far do Sources A and B support the view that the Matteotti crisis was the turning point in the creation of the Fascist dictatorship?
items.answer: Source A supports: it marks the move from coalition government to dictatorship after the crisis. Evaluation: it is a political performance designed to intimidate. Source B challenges: it suggests the support of elites, not the crisis itself, was decisive. Evaluation: it is a private view, perhaps written in despair. Grouping: support A; challenge B. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.

items.stem: ‘Mussolini's foreign policy was driven mainly by a desire for prestige.’ How far do you agree?
items.answer: For: Corfu, Abyssinia and Albania were showy, opportunistic actions. Propaganda presented foreign policy as national greatness. He joined the war in 1940 to share in victory. Against: He pursued consistent aims of Mediterranean and African expansion. He sought security, as at the Brenner in 1934 and Stresa. Ideology drew him to Germany and against communism in Spain. Judgement: prestige was a constant motive, but it served a consistent goal of making Italy the dominant Mediterranean power.

items.stem: On 28 October 1922 Fascist squads converged on Rome; King Victor Emmanuel III refused to declare martial law. Analyse the reasons why Mussolini became prime minister in October 1922.
items.answer: The Liberal governments were weak and unstable. Fear of socialism after the biennio rosso won support from landowners, industrialists and the middle class. Fascist violence destroyed socialist organisations while the police looked on. Mussolini combined violence with negotiation and appeared respectable. The king and elites chose to bring him into government rather than resist. Judgement: Mussolini came to power because the elites, fearing socialism and lacking confidence in Liberal government, chose to appoint him.

items.stem: Tomás is planning an answer to the question: “How far was the March on Rome a bluff?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Tomás could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the march was a bluff militarily, but the threat it represented was real enough to persuade the king to give way. Support: The squads were poorly armed and could have been dispersed by the army. Mussolini stayed in Milan, near the Swiss border. Challenge: The threat of violence was real and had been demonstrated. Fascists had seized control of many northern towns.

items.stem: Study Sources B and C. Source B: a report by a prefect in the Po valley, 1921 (illustrative). “The Fascist squads move by lorry from town to town, burning the offices of the leagues. The carabinieri watch and do nothing; the landowners pay for the petrol.” Source C: a speech by Mussolini, Naples, 24 October 1922 (summary). Mussolini told the Fascist congress that either the government would be given to the Fascists or they would take it by marching on Rome. To what extent do Sources B and C agree about the rise of Fascism?
items.answer: Source B: It suggests that squads acted with the support of landowners and the tolerance of the authorities. Source C: It shows Mussolini threatening force to gain power. They disagree about whether Mussolini came to power mainly because of the weakness of the Liberal state; similarities and differences should be supported with details. Provenance: B is a report by a prefect in the Po valley, 1921 (illustrative) (a prefect may have exaggerated to explain his failure to keep order); C is a speech by Mussolini, Naples, 24 October 1922 (summary) (it was intended to intimidate and may not reflect his real plans). Differences in authorship, date and purpose explain the contrast.
items.markingKey: Level 4 (12-15): compares and contrasts the sources, explaining similarities AND differences, and evaluates them using provenance and context to explain why they differ. Level 3 (8-11): explains similarities AND differences in content, supported by details from both sources. Level 2 (4-7): explains a similarity OR a difference. Level 1 (1-3): describes or paraphrases the content of the sources without valid comparison. [15]
